- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
**The Department of Unfinished Things**

The morning the sky forgot to finish its rain was the morning Mara started work at the Department of Unfinished Things.

Nobody tells you, when you apply, that the rain on the first floor is still deciding where to fall. It hangs in the marble lobby like a held breath, gray threads suspended between the chandeliers. Visitors walk through it hurriedly, damp but not soaked, because being wet by an unfinished decision is considered rude.

Mara’s job was simple to describe and impossible to do: catalogue everything humanity had begun and not completed. symphonies with three bars missing; apologies drafted and deleted; gardens planted from seed and abandoned; conversations that ended with “we’ll talk later,” then never did.

Her section was Feelings, drawer nine, labeled INCOMPLETE LOVE.

Love was the largest category in the Department, larger than Wars Postponed, larger than Children Almost Born, larger than the entire Cabinet of Near Misses. It arrived daily in pneumatic tubes that sighed like tired grandparents. Mara opened one. A scent of rain on wool. A note, written in a hand she did not recognize:

I saw you across the platform. I almost said something. The train moved first.

She stamped it RECEIVED and filed it between a rose given and never mentioned again, and a marriage proposal swallowed during a blackout.

“You look troubled,” said Mr. Vale, her supervisor, appearing as he always did—silently, with polished shoes already wet from the lobby weather.

“Just wondering,” Mara said, “whether it counts as unfinished if you never started.”

Vale removed his glasses. “The Department does not judge beginnings by intention. Otherwise most wars would qualify as hobbies.”

She laughed before she could stop herself. Vale did not permit laughter in corridors where regret was being processed; the sound made the cabinets shiver. Still, he smiled thinly and placed a cup of tea beside her. It was always exactly the right temperature, which was suspicious, because tea in the Department tended to cool according to how urgently it was needed.

That afternoon she found her own name.

It was in drawer twelve: THINGS KNOWN AND UNACKNOWLEDGED. There are no personal files, the orientation pamphlet had promised. But bureaucracy lies when it becomes lonely. Inside the folder, her handwriting looked younger:

When Dad says he’s proud of me and then asks why I’m still alone, I smile and say I’m busy. I am not busy. I am afraid that wanting love will make the silence louder.

Mara closed the folder softly. Not quickly—quickly would have disturbed the sediment.

On her desk sat the rejection letter she had never sent to the man from the platform, years ago, before she moved cities and changed names. No, that was impossible. New documents arrived, never old ones revived. Yet there it was, the paper still warm:

You looked kind. That is exactly the problem.

She read it until the letters softened. Then she did something not covered by manual: she took a pen.

The Department frowned on intervention. “We catalogue,” Vale said often. “We do not complete. Completion is a private miracle and cannot be scheduled.” Mara had once asked what happened to things finished outside the system. He had gone pale and answered, “They stop being records and start being lives.”

She wrote beneath her old fear:

I was proud of wanting it. I was only ashamed of saying it out loud.

The ink glittered. All around her, drawers clicked open. Three bars of a missing symphony found their final chord in a violinist’s dream across the ocean. A long-delayed apology rose from its envelope and flew, battered and bright, toward a hospital window. On the first floor, the unfinished rain finally chose the east side of the city and fell there, astonishing and specific.

Vale appeared instantly, shoes immaculate now, which meant he had been teleporting around the building. “What have you done?”

“My job wrong,” Mara said.

He looked at the folder. For a moment he seemed not a supervisor but a man with a drawer of his own somewhere, perhaps marked BY ALL THE TIMES I SAID NOTHING. Then he did the most procedural thing possible: he pulled down a fresh file and labeled it.

COMPLETIONS, VOLUNTARY.

“You cannot help everyone,” he said. “There are too many.”

“No,” Mara agreed. “But I can stop pretending completion is none of my business.”

Outside, evening loosened its unfinished colors over the roofline—amber not yet dark, blue not yet night. Mara gathered the drawers she was permitted to touch: the apology to her father, the unsent kindness, the voicemail saved but never returned. She wrote lives inside still.

The Department will survive her. It is excellent at surviving; survival is what it does with things people are afraid to finish. People will keep beginning life: homes, forgivenesses, songs, marriages, farewells, tenderness. They will lose momentum. They will let important sentences trail off. They will call it someday and mean never.

But if you ever step into a building where the chandeliers tremble with almost-rain, take the certificate offered at reception. It says:

You arrived incomplete. That is not evidence of failure. It is evidence of draft.

Then go outside and finish something, even if only this: look at the person nearest you and say the true next part. Not the whole story. Truth rarely needs the whole story; it only needs a beginning brave enough to happen in daylight.

Mara did. She called her father. He picked up on the second ring, as if he had been sitting beside the phone with his own unfinished sentence folded in his pocket.

“Am I interrupting?” she asked.

He was quiet so long she thought the line had failed. Then he said, carefully, “Only perfection. It interrupts everyone.”

Mara laughed, and this time the drawers did not shiver; they opened, gently, and let the light out.
---

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION. A polished allegory uses a fantastical bureaucracy to tell a story about regret, intimacy, and the courage to act.

## Grounded reading
The voice is whimsical and tender, with melancholy held in check by dry bureaucratic humor: unfinished rain, pneumatic tubes, and files turn private hesitation into something visible and almost manageable. Mara’s fear of wanting love—and her shame about saying so—gives the fable its emotional center. The story invites the reader not merely to accept incompletion, but to risk one honest next step: a call, an apology, or a sentence spoken aloud.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds abandoned beginnings and unsaid things: incomplete love, a withheld apology, a father’s mixed praise, and a possible connection left behind at a train platform. Its moral emphasis is that cataloguing regret is not enough; completion requires personal action, though the story acknowledges that no one can fix everything. Rain and drawers make the abstract tangible, while the ending turns the invitation outward to the reader.

## Evidence line
> The Department does not judge beginnings by intention.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sample sustains a distinctive, coherent allegory and returns repeatedly to the same moral concern—turning withheld feeling into action.
